mcp-spice 0.1 (zesun33)

features.note: From each project's public page on 9 Nov 2026 (ltspice-mcp: PyPI page; mcp-spice: Glama listing; spicebridge: search listing only, its page did not load). Not run here: installing third-party packages was blocked in this sandbox. Treat 'not stated' as unknown, not as missing.

headline: With a smaller model (Haiku 5.5), SpiceMCP is the only way the buck converter worked. Haiku alone and Haiku with a raw simulator both produced bucks that miss 5 V ±2% or the ripple limit (0 of 30 boards); Haiku driving SpiceMCP got 30 of 30.

With a strong model (Opus 5.5), all three approaches met every spec at nominal on all three circuits. For simple, well-known circuits a strong model already writes the textbook answer, and SpiceMCP did not beat it on pass rate or yield.
The RC filter caps out near 40% for everyone: ±2% cutoff with 5% capacitors is not buildable reliably. Both SpiceMCP runs said so and named the fix (tighter capacitor).
Amplifier: Haiku with SpiceMCP reached 91.5% yield by re-optimising to a centred pair (102k / 11.3k); the scripted Opus run took SpiceMCP's first answer and got 66.5%. Haiku alone got 65%.

What SpiceMCP costs: it is the slowest (buck yield check about 14 min) and Haiku made 44 tool calls, 23 of them repeated 'still running' polls. Haiku with a raw simulator used 4 times the output tokens (146k vs 35k) and still failed the buck.
honest: With a strong model, this benchmark does not show that SpiceMCP designs better circuits. On these three it designs about the same circuits; its value is the measured yield, standard values, ratings and drawings.

With a smaller model it clearly does: the closed-loop buck is out of Haiku's reach without it (two different failed designs: one settles slowly and sits 0.1 to 0.2 V low, one is 0.8 to 1 V high with 0.5 V ripple), and in reach with it.

Haiku also stayed honest with SpiceMCP: it reported the RC filter as not meeting spec at 41% yield instead of claiming a pass. Haiku alone gave itself 'high confidence' on RC and amp and only 'low-medium' on the buck, which failed.
Both no-tool bucks and the Haiku raw-simulator buck used an ideal switch, which is not a part you can buy. The checker does not punish idealisations; a stricter benchmark should.
All arms were handed SpiceMCP's own working op-amp and comparator models. That removes the hardest part of the buck for the baselines, so the buck result still flatters them.
The Opus SpiceMCP arm was driven by a script, not a model; the Haiku SpiceMCP arm was driven by the model itself through a bridge to the real server. The Haiku run is the fairer test of the tool.
fixes: finish_design should centre ratios, not just snap each value: search standard-value pairs for the one closest to the middle of the limits. On the amplifier that lifts yield from 66.5% to 91%.

Do not shrink parts to the edge by default: the 'smallest capacitor / inductor' goals left the buck at 44 mV worst-case ripple against a 50 mV limit. Aim for the middle of the limit, or give the user the size-vs-margin choice.

Make long finishes cheaper to wait for: the buck needed 13 (script) and 23 (Haiku) identical 'still running' polls. Return an estimated finish time and tell the model to wait that long, or report progress instead.
Say 'not buildable at this tolerance' up front: when the spec window is narrower than the part tolerance (RC ±2% with 5% capacitors), say so before optimising.
limits: Three circuits, one run per model and arm; runs are not repeated, so luck is not averaged out.

Simulation only (ngspice 42). The buck ripple needs a 2 ns time step to be honest: at 20 ns SpiceMCP's buck reads 180 mV. The raw-simulator buck only runs at 20 ns or 5 ns, so its ripple number is less certain.
Buck yield is 30 boards per arm (90 runs at three temperatures): 30/30 means at least 90% with 95% confidence. RC and amplifier use 200 boards.
Tokens are counted with an older public tokenizer and exclude the tool harness's own system prompt, which is the same for every arm.

about: Same spec text, same parts file, same checker and the same random boards as the Opus run. Every design call was made by claude-haiku-5-5 (checked in the transcripts); Opus only checked the results and wrote this report.

SpiceMCP arm: Haiku saw the real tool list and called the real server through a small shell bridge (measure/bridge.py) that keeps one MCP session open and logs every call. It chose its own calls: templates, re-optimising, finish, simulate.
Raw-simulator arm: Haiku wrote netlists and ran ngspice itself (22 runs). No-tool arm: Haiku wrote the netlists from memory.
